compareCandidate.label: Virus vs. bacterium
compareCandidate.description: A virus is not a cell - it holds only genetic material in a protein coat and needs a host to copy itself. A bacterium is a living single-celled organism that can divide on its own. That is why they differ hugely.

processes: Forcing the host to copy the virus
Being fought by the immune system
plainLanguageExplanation: A virus is the smallest kind of infectious agent. It is not a cell and it is not living in the usual sense - it is basically a package of genetic material (DNA or RNA) wrapped inside a protein coat, sometimes with spikes. It cannot grow, eat, or reproduce on its own. Instead, it must find a living cell and get inside. Then it commandeers that cell's machinery to copy the virus, making many new viruses that can then infect more cells. That is how a viral infection spreads through the body, until the immune system attacks the viruses.

keyFacts.label: Treatment note
keyFacts.value: Our immune system responds to them; antibiotics do not

whyItMatters: Viruses cause many illnesses from the common cold to flu, and understanding them explains infection, vaccines, and why antibiotics won't work on them. Since a virus is not a cell, it needs special handling - which is why we learn about them distinctly from bacteria.
tagline: A tiny virus that needs a host to copy itself
didYouKnow: A single virus particle is so small you would need thousands of them to span the width of a single typical cell.
